front: What is the difference between commercial and non-commercial energy? Give an example of each.
back: Commercial energy is traded at a market price (coal, oil, natural gas, grid electricity); non-commercial energy is not normally bought and sold (firewood, cattle dung, agricultural waste).
explain: Commercial sources power industry, transport and urban households and are the basis of national energy statistics. Non-commercial sources are gathered free, mainly in rural areas, and are often left out of official consumption figures. Solar energy used for water heating is also treated as non-commercial in BEE questions.
source: BEE 2024 P1 S7; BEE 2025 P1 Q44

front: Distinguish primary and secondary energy sources.
back: Primary energy is found or stored in nature (coal, crude oil, natural gas, biomass, solar, wind, hydro, nuclear fuel); secondary energy is produced by converting primary energy (electricity, steam, petrol/diesel from refining).
explain: Primary sources are mostly converted in industrial utilities into secondary forms before end use. For example, coal is burnt in a power station to make electricity, and crude oil is refined into transport fuels. Every conversion step has losses, so saving one unit of secondary energy saves more than one unit of primary energy.

front: Distinguish renewable and non-renewable energy, with an example of each.
back: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished and practically inexhaustible (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal); non-renewable energy comes from finite stocks that run out over time (coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel).
explain: Renewables are generally low-carbon and do not deplete. Fossil fuels took millions of years to form and are being used up much faster than they form. Coal is the standard 'non-renewable' answer in BEE objective questions.

front: How is the Reserves-to-Production (R/P) ratio calculated, and what does it tell you?
back: R/P = reserves remaining at the end of the year ÷ production in that year. It gives the number of years the remaining reserves would last if production continued at that rate.
explain: India's coal R/P ratio is much higher than its oil and gas R/P ratios. That is why coal is seen as the fuel that can give secure domestic supply for decades, while oil and gas depend heavily on imports. The ratio changes as new reserves are found or production rises.
source: BEE 2024 P1 Q34; BEE 2025 P1 Q34

front: Define energy intensity.
back: Energy intensity = Energy consumption ÷ GDP (for example, toe per million US$ of GDP). It shows how much energy the economy uses to produce one unit of economic output.
explain: High energy intensity means energy is being turned into GDP inefficiently, or that the economy relies on energy-heavy industry. Low energy intensity usually means energy is being turned into GDP efficiently. It is a macro indicator used to compare countries over time.
source: BEE 2024 P1 Q23; BEE 2025 P1 S2

front: Why does a lower energy intensity not necessarily mean higher energy efficiency?
back: Energy intensity also depends on economic structure (share of services against heavy industry), climate, geography, lifestyle, exchange rates and how much non-commercial energy is counted. It is not only technical efficiency.
explain: A service-led economy can have low energy intensity even with inefficient equipment. A country with a large steel or cement base can show high intensity even with efficient plants. Energy intensity is therefore only a rough proxy for efficiency.

front: Why is GDP converted using Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) when comparing energy intensity across countries?
back: PPP values every country's GDP at a uniform price level. The comparison then reflects differences in real economic volume, not market exchange-rate distortions.
explain: Market exchange rates undervalue the output of developing countries, where many goods and services are cheaper. GDP at market exchange rates therefore makes their energy intensity look much higher than it really is. PPP-based GDP gives a fairer comparison.
source: BEE 2024 P1 S6; BEE 2025 P1 Q35

front: How are energy conservation and energy efficiency related?
back: Energy efficiency means using less energy for the same output or service (lower energy per unit). Energy conservation means reducing overall energy consumption, which can include behaviour change or doing without.
explain: Efficiency is about technology and how well equipment performs, such as an efficient motor doing the same work with less input. Conservation is broader: it includes efficiency and also avoiding waste, such as switching off idle equipment. Both cut demand, and efficiency does not require reducing comfort or output.

front: Why is energy saved through Demand Side Management (DSM) treated like new supply-side capacity?
back: Each MW of demand avoided by DSM does the same job as adding a MW of generation (a 'negawatt'), and it costs much less than building new power plants.
explain: DSM programmes run by utilities or DISCOMs shift or reduce load, especially at peak, through efficient appliances, time-of-day tariffs and load management. The aims are to lower peak demand, defer capital spending on capacity, and improve the load factor. Increasing generator load to meet the peak is NOT a DSM objective.
source: BEE 2025 P1 Q1; BEE 2024 P1 Q10

front: What was the main aim of India's Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme (APDRP)?
back: To reduce Aggregate Technical & Commercial (AT&C) losses in distribution through energy accounting and audits, metering, and strengthening of the sub-transmission and distribution network.
explain: AT&C losses combine technical losses (I²R in lines and transformers) with commercial losses (theft, unmetered supply, billing and collection gaps). APDRP and its restructured successor (R-APDRP) funded IT-based energy accounting and network upgrades for state utilities.

front: Why was Availability Based Tariff (ABT) introduced in India?
back: To improve grid discipline and frequency control. It does this with a tariff of three parts: a capacity (fixed) charge, an energy (variable) charge, and an Unscheduled Interchange (UI) charge linked to frequency.
explain: Under ABT, a generator is paid its capacity charge for the availability it declares, and its energy charge for energy actually scheduled. Deviations from schedule are priced by grid frequency: over-drawing at low frequency is expensive. This rewards keeping to schedule and supporting frequency.

front: Country X consumes 500 Mtoe of energy and has a GDP of US$ 2.5 trillion. Country Y consumes 300 Mtoe and has a GDP of US$ 1.2 trillion. Calculate the energy intensity of each in toe per million US$ and state which uses energy more productively.
back: X: 200 toe per million US$; Y: 250 toe per million US$. Country X has the lower energy intensity.
explain: Energy intensity = energy ÷ GDP, so a lower value means more GDP per unit of energy. Before concluding that X is more energy efficient, remember that economic structure, climate and PPP effects also affect intensity.

steps.answer: X: 2.5 trillion = 2,500,000 million US$; Y: 1.2 trillion = 1,200,000 million US$.
X: 500×10⁶ ÷ 2.5×10⁶ = 200 toe/million US$; Y: 300×10⁶ ÷ 1.2×10⁶ = 250 toe/million US$.
X has the lower EI, so it produces more GDP per toe.
steps.explain: Lower intensity suggests better productivity of energy use, but is not by itself proof of technical efficiency.

front: By roughly what percentage does global energy demand grow each year, and what share of primary energy comes from fossil fuels?
back: About 2.4% per year; over 85% of primary energy comes from fossil fuels.
explain: The guide book opens the chapter with these two numbers to show why the present pattern of use, especially of oil, cannot last. Demand keeps rising while the resource base is finite, so efficiency and conservation become a necessity rather than an option.

front: Arrange the forms of coal in order of increasing rank (age/carbon content), starting from peat.
back: Peat → brown coal (lignite) → sub-bituminous → bituminous → anthracite.
explain: Coal forms as plant matter is buried and transformed by heat and pressure over time (Figure 1.3). Lignite is the youngest and lowest-grade true coal; anthracite has the highest carbon content. The BP tables group reserves as 'anthracite and bituminous' and 'sub-bituminous and lignite'.

front: What were the world's proven coal reserves at the end of 2013, and how long would they last at the then production rate?
back: About 892 billion tonnes (891,531 million t), enough for about 113 years (BP Statistical Review 2014).
explain: Coal is the most abundant and most widely spread fossil fuel, with recoverable reserves in around 75 countries. The 113-year figure is the world R/P ratio at end-2013 production. It is a common objective question: 'coal on our planet is expected to last about 113 years'.

front: True or false: once established, a fuel's Reserves-to-Production (R/P) ratio stays constant.
back: False. The R/P ratio changes every year because both reserves (new finds, revisions) and production change.
explain: R/P = reserves remaining at the end of a year ÷ production in that year. It tells you how long reserves would last if production stayed at that year's level. New discoveries raise the numerator and rising output raises the denominator, so the ratio is recomputed every year.

front: Which five countries held the largest proven coal reserves at the end of 2013 (in order)?
back: USA (26.6%), Russia (17.6%), China (12.8%), Australia (8.6%), India (6.8%).
explain: From Table 1.1 (BP 2014): USA ~237 billion t, Russia ~157, China ~114.5, Australia ~76.4, India ~60.6 billion t. China's R/P was only about 31 years because its output is enormous, while India's was about 100 years.

front: Which country was the world's largest coal producer in 2013, and roughly what share did it have?
back: China, about 3,680 million tonnes, roughly 47% of world output (2013).
explain: World coal production in 2013 was about 7,896 million t. The US came second with about 893 Mt. India produced about 605 Mt. The book notes China alone now uses as much coal as the rest of the world, and most coal demand comes from the power sector.

front: What were the world's proven crude oil reserves at the end of 2013, and roughly what share lay in the Middle East?
back: About 1,687.9 billion barrels, with almost 48% in the Middle East (BP 2014).
explain: Table 1.3 lists Venezuela (298.3 bn bbl, 17.7%) and Saudi Arabia (265.9 bn bbl, 15.8%) at the top, followed by Canada, Iran and Iraq. India had only about 5.7 billion barrels (0.3%). The world R/P for oil at end-2013 was about 53 years.

front: About how many litres are in one barrel of oil?
back: About 160 litres (1 barrel ≈ 159 L, rounded to 160 L in the guide book).
explain: Oil reserves and production are quoted in barrels internationally and in tonnes in Indian statistics. Remembering the conversion helps when you move between the two, together with the oil's density.

front: Which country was the largest oil producer in 2013, and what is notable about the United States' position?
back: Saudi Arabia (≈542 Mt/yr, 13.1%), closely followed by Russia and the US. The US ranked third in production but only tenth in proven reserves.
explain: World oil output in 2013 was about 4,130 Mt. India produced about 42 Mt, about 1% of the total. A big producer with small reserves depletes faster, which is why the book warns that many non-Middle-East producers could largely deplete their fields and the world may come to depend on the Middle East.

front: What is the average R/P ratio of Middle East conventional oil, and how much would global oil reserves grow if unconventional oil is counted?
back: About 78 years for the Middle East; counting unconventional oil would make global reserves about four times larger than current conventional reserves.
explain: Unconventional resources include oil shale, oil sands, extra heavy oil and natural bitumen. The book expects oil's main use to shift towards transport and petrochemicals, and its top position to be challenged by natural gas.

front: Distinguish oil shale and oil sands (tar sands).
back: Oil shale is sedimentary rock containing solid bituminous material (kerogen) that releases petroleum-like liquid when heated (pyrolysis). Oil sands are a mix of clay, sand, water and bitumen, mined and processed to extract the bitumen, which is refined into oil.
explain: Both are 'unconventional' oil. The difference is that oil shale holds kerogen that must be chemically converted by heating, while oil sands already contain heavy viscous bitumen that is separated and then upgraded.

front: What were the world's proven natural gas reserves at the end of 2013, how many years would they last, and which three countries held the most?
back: About 186 trillion m³ (185.7), roughly 55 years of production; Iran (18.2%), Russia (16.8%) and Qatar (13.3%). India had about 0.7%.
explain: Natural gas is mainly methane with small amounts of ethane, propane, butane and pentane, and it is processed to remove almost everything except methane before use. It ranks third in use after oil and coal. Like oil, its reserves are concentrated in a few countries and fields.

front: What was global primary energy consumption in 2013, and what were the shares of oil, coal and natural gas?
back: About 12,730 Mtoe; oil 33%, coal 30%, natural gas 24% (hydro 7%, nuclear 4%, renewables 2%).
explain: From Table 1.6 (BP 2014). Note the text says 'end of 2014' for the same 12,730 Mtoe figure but the source is BP June 2014, so it is really 2013 data. Gas demand is expected to grow as industrial countries act to cut CO₂ emissions.

front: Which country was the largest energy consumer in 2013, and how did India's consumption compare?
back: China (about 2,852 Mtoe, 22.4% of world). India's 595 Mtoe was about 4.7% of the world, 26% of the USA's and 21% of China's consumption (2013).
explain: The USA was second at about 2,266 Mtoe (17.8%). A common exam trap is to answer 'USA'. India's absolute consumption is small relative to its population, as the per-capita figures in the chapter also show.

front: How is 'final energy consumption' defined, and what is excluded from it?
back: It is the energy available to end users after conversion from primary energy: the sum of consumption in the end-use sectors. Energy used for transformation and for own use by energy-producing industries is excluded.
explain: Final consumption therefore reflects energy actually delivered to consumers. Globally, industry uses almost 50% of final energy, then transport (20%), residential (18%) and commercial (12%) (US EIA figures quoted in the book).

front: What was India's primary commercial energy consumption mix in 2013?
back: Total 595 Mtoe: coal 54.5%, oil 29.5%, natural gas 7.8%, hydro 5.0%, renewables 2.0%, nuclear 1.3% (Table 1.8).
explain: Coal dominates both India's production and consumption. Oil is the second-largest source and is mostly imported. Gas's share in India (7.8%) is far below the world average of about 24%.

front: In India, roughly what shares of total primary energy consumption come from commercial and non-commercial energy?
back: Commercial about 74%; non-commercial about 26%.
explain: Non-commercial energy (firewood, cattle dung, agricultural waste) is mostly used in rural households and is often left out of energy statistics, so it is easy to underestimate. The figure shows how much India still relies on traditional fuels.

front: What are India's coal reserves, and how long might they last at the current R/P ratio?
back: About 60.6 billion t (hard coal 56.1 bn t, soft coal 4.5 bn t), about 6.8% of world reserves, enough for about 100 years. Jharkhand and Odisha hold almost 51% (as of 31 March 2013).
explain: Indian reserves are concentrated in the eastern and south-central parts of the country. Hard coal means anthracite and bituminous; soft coal means sub-bituminous and lignite.

front: State three characteristics of Indian coal mining and coal quality mentioned in the guide book.
back: Over 80% is mined by open-cast mining (up to 150–300 m depth). The coal has high ash (30–45%) and a calorific value of about 3,000–4,500 kcal/kg. The power sector uses about 75% of the coal produced.
explain: High-ash coal makes efficient combustion and fly-ash management hard for power stations. That is why higher-CV, low-ash coal is imported, mainly from Indonesia, Australia and South Africa, and coking coal is imported by the steel sector.

front: What is the Clean Energy Cess on coal, since when has it applied, and at what rate (as stated in the book)?
back: A tax of Rs 100 per tonne on all coal, peat and lignite mined in India or imported, levied since 1 July 2010.
explain: The cess raises funds for research, development and deployment of cleaner and renewable energy technologies. Exam MCQs ask which fuel carries it: the answer is coal, not electricity or diesel. The rate is as given in the 2015 guide book.

front: How much coal did India import in 2012-13, what share of requirement was this, and who were the main suppliers?
back: About 145.8 million t (≈20% of annual requirement) in 2012-13, mainly from Indonesia, then Australia and South Africa.
explain: Imports rose sharply after 2011 (68.9 Mt in 2010-11, 102.9 Mt in 2011-12). Steel makers import coking coal for quality reasons. Coastal power stations and cement plants import non-coking coal for logistics and cost.

front: What carbon-intensity commitment had India made, according to the guide book?
back: To reduce the carbon intensity of its economy by 20–25% from 2005 levels by 2020 (a domestic commitment).
explain: The book notes that relying on coal for large-scale rural electrification could make it harder to meet this target. Carbon intensity is emissions per unit of GDP, not total emissions.

front: Summarise India's oil position as given in the guide book (reserves, share, main fields, R/P, import dependence).
back: Reserves about 5.7 bn barrels (800 Mt), only ~0.3% of world reserves. Main fields are Bombay High, upper Assam, Cambay and the Krishna-Godavari basin. R/P is about 17.5 years, and India imports over 75% of its crude.
explain: Production was about 42 Mt against consumption of about 175 Mt (2013). India was the fourth-largest oil consumer. Transport is the biggest user of petroleum products, followed by domestic and industry. Crude imports in 2013-14 were 189.2 Mt costing about Rs 8.65 lakh crore.

front: To what temperature is natural gas cooled to make LNG, and by how much does liquefaction shrink its volume?
back: About −161 °C; liquefaction cuts the volume about 600 times.
explain: LNG is shipped in special cryogenic tankers and regasified at receiving terminals. By contrast, CNG is natural gas compressed to under 1% of its atmospheric volume and stored in cylinders at about 200–248 kg/cm². It can run converted petrol (bi-fuel) vehicles.

front: Summarise India's natural gas position: reserves, R/P, share of consumption, and main consuming sectors.
back: Reserves about 1.4 trillion m³ (0.7% of world); R/P about 40 years; gas is about 7.8% of India's fuel consumption versus a world average of about 24% (2013). Power generation and fertiliser use about 62% of gas.
explain: About 66% of Indian gas comes from offshore fields; onshore output is mainly from Assam, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh. Consumption (51.4 bcm) exceeded production (33.7 bcm) in 2013, so LNG is imported. The drawbacks the book lists are price unpredictability and uncertain availability.

front: What was India's installed power capacity in February 2014, and how was it split?
back: About 2,38,743 MW: thermal 1,63,305 MW (68.4%; coal 58.9%, gas 9.0%), hydro 40,195 MW (16.8%), renewables 29,463 MW (12.3%), nuclear 5,780 MW (2.4%).
explain: Thermal power is the major source of electricity generation in India. Gross generation in 2013-14 was about 881,786 million kWh, and the country faced an energy shortage of 3.8% and a peak shortage of 3.3% (Ministry of Power).

front: Why is India's ability to develop nuclear power restricted?
back: Indian uranium ore contains only about 0.1% uranium, compared with 12–13% in ores mined abroad. Domestic uranium can support only about 10,000 MW of nuclear capacity.
explain: In 2015 India ran 21 nuclear units at seven locations totalling 5,780 MW (BWRs and PHWRs), about 2% of installed capacity. The Department of Atomic Energy planned 63,000 MW by 2032. The MCQ answer to 'nuclear development is constrained by…' is 'all of the above': low ore grade, inadequate supply and import constraints.

front: What is India's economically viable hydro potential, and where is most of it?
back: Over 84,000 MW at 60% load factor, about 80% of it in the Brahmaputra, Indus and Ganges basins, plus about 15,000 MW in small hydro.
explain: Hydro's share of generated units had fallen to about 17% by 2013. To speed up development, projects up to 25 MW were placed under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), while larger projects stay with the Ministry of Power.

front: Which sector consumes the largest share of India's commercial energy, and which comes next?
back: Industry, about 44%, followed by transport (about 17%) (Figure 1.4, TERI).
explain: Specific energy consumption in major Indian industries is well above global benchmarks. For example, iron and steel uses 25.5–34.2 GJ/t in India against 16.5–18.5 GJ/t worldwide, and aluminium 75.6–83.2 versus 70.5–73.0 GJ/t (Table 1.13). That gap is the efficiency opportunity.

front: What growth rate and share of petroleum products does the guide book give for India's transport sector, and what is the 2030 projection?
back: It grows about 16% a year and uses around 40% of petroleum products. By 2030, road vehicles are projected to take 86% of transport energy, aviation 9%, and rail, marine and others 5%.
explain: This is why mass transport, fuel-efficiency standards and moving freight to railways appear in the energy-security and integrated-energy-policy measures.

front: How do rural and urban households meet their cooking needs, and how is domestic electricity used?
back: Rural households meet about 85% of cooking needs from biomass; urban households meet about 56% from LPG. About 70% of domestic electricity is used for lighting, and the remaining 30% for refrigeration, air-conditioning and gadgets.
explain: About 70% of India's population is rural but accounts for only about 42% of demand for oil, gas and electricity. The high lighting share explains why lamp programmes such as BLY and LED replacement were early priorities.

front: What was India's per-capita electricity consumption in 2012-13, and how did it compare with the world average?
back: About 917 kWh per person per year, against a world average of about 2,430 kWh.
explain: It rose from 819 kWh (2010-11) to 884 kWh (2011-12) and 917 kWh (2012-13) (CEA). Comparable figures quoted are the USA 13,246, Canada 16,473, Japan 7,848, UK 6,206 and China 3,298 kWh.

front: To sustain 8% GDP growth up to 2031-32, how much must India's energy supply grow?
back: Primary energy supply 3–4 times, electricity installed capacity 6–7 times, and annual coal requirement nearly 3 times (to over 2 billion t/yr).
explain: These targets come from the Integrated Energy Policy. Oil import dependence was expected to rise from about 75% to over 90%, and the share of natural gas was expected to reach 20–25% by 2030-32.

front: What did the Accelerated Power Development & Reform Programme (2002-03) target for AT&C losses, and what did its restructured version (R-APDRP) focus on?
back: It targeted reducing Aggregate Technical & Commercial (AT&C) losses to 15%. R-APDRP focuses on actual, demonstrable performance in loss reduction.
explain: APDRP used technical, commercial, financial and IT interventions to improve reliability and supply quality, revenue collection and the commercial viability of State Electricity Boards. The book says capacity would have to double every 10 years to sustain growth.

front: How did India's industrial/commercial electricity tariff compare internationally on a PPP basis, and how is it set?
back: About 30.8 US cents/kWh (PPP), against 7.7 in the US, 15.3 in Japan and 20.6 in China. Tariffs are set by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions on a cost-plus basis, with industry and commerce cross-subsidising agriculture and domestic users.
explain: HT consumers pay for both demand (kVA) and energy (kWh), while LT consumers usually pay for energy (kWh) only. Flat-rate supply to farm pumps based on horsepower means zero marginal cost, which encourages inefficient use and over-exploitation of groundwater.

front: List the key features of Availability Based Tariff (ABT).
back: A performance-based tariff for central generating stations. A scheduling and dispatch system in which generators and beneficiaries commit to day-ahead schedules. Rewards and penalties enforce those schedules, with changes allowed if notified 1.5 hours in advance. It also emphasises prompt payment of dues.
explain: ABT and unscheduled interchange (UI) charges were introduced in 2003 for inter-state power sale and have reduced voltage and frequency fluctuations. ABT applies to electricity, which is a frequent MCQ.

front: How does the guide book (quoting UNDP's World Energy Assessment 1999) define energy security?
back: 'The continuous availability of energy in varied forms in sufficient quantities at reasonable prices.'
explain: For a nation, the basic aim is to reduce dependence on imported energy for economic growth. India's concern is acute because about 75% of oil is imported, mostly from the volatile Middle East, and oil demand was rising about 5% a year from domestic wells over 30 years old.

front: Name the four broad strategies the guide book gives for meeting India's future energy requirements.
back: 1) Reduce energy requirements. 2) Substitute imported oil/gas with domestic alternatives. 3) Diversify energy supply sources. 4) Expand the energy resource base and develop alternative sources.
explain: Examples: efficient supercritical boilers, DSM and mass transport (reduce). Ethanol/biodiesel, biomass gasification and coal-to-oil (substitute). A fuel mix with no single dependence and oil/LNG from several countries (diversify). IOR/EOR, coal-bed methane, in-situ coal gasification and thorium reactors (expand).

front: Name the benefits of energy efficiency at the levels of industry, nation and globe (Figure 1.7).
back: Industry: lower energy bills, more competitiveness, productivity and profit, better quality. Nation: lower energy imports, avoided costs used for poverty reduction, conservation of limited resources, better energy security. Globe: less GHG and other emissions, a sustainable environment.
explain: Energy efficiency has been practised since the 1973 oil crisis but now matters more as the most cost-effective way to mitigate climate change. Industry accounts for about 41% of global primary energy demand and a similar share of CO₂ emissions.

front: Convert into tonnes of oil equivalent: (a) 10,000 kg of coal with a calorific value of 4,000 kcal/kg; (b) 10 lakh kWh of electricity.
back: (a) 4 toe; (b) 86 toe.
explain: 1 toe = 1 × 10⁷ kcal = 11,630 kWh. Multiply quantity by calorific value to get kcal and divide by 10⁷. For electricity, use 1 kWh = 860 kcal (equivalently divide kWh by 11,630).

steps.explain: This is the standard conversion given in Section 1.2.

steps.prompt: Find the heat content of the coal.

steps.explain: Both routes give the same answer.

front: India's coal reserves at the end of 2013 were about 60,600 million t and production about 605 million t. Estimate the R/P ratio and interpret it.
back: R/P ≈ 100 years. If production stayed at the 2013 level, reserves would last about 100 years.
explain: R/P = reserves remaining at the end of the year ÷ that year's production. The answer matches the book's statement that Indian coal may last about 100 years. It is only a snapshot: rising production or new discoveries change the ratio every year.

steps.answer: R/P (years) = reserves at end of year ÷ production in that year
Reserves would last about 100 years at constant 2013 output
steps.explain: R/P assumes production stays at the current level.

front: An egg costs Rs 3 in India and 30 yen in Japan (30 yen ≈ Rs 15 at the market exchange rate). Find the PPP rate for eggs and explain why using the market rate would mislead.
back: PPP = 30 yen / Rs 3 = 10 yen per rupee. The market rate (2 yen per rupee here) would overstate Japan's GDP relative to India's, because Japan's price level is higher.
explain: A PPP exchange rate equalises the purchasing power of currencies for the same basket of goods. Using PPP values all countries' GDP at a uniform price level, so comparisons reflect real volume of output. That is why energy intensity is often given in kgoe per US$ (PPP) of GDP.

steps.prompt: Set up the PPP ratio for the same good.
steps.answer: PPP = price in Japan / price in India = 30 yen / Rs 3
steps.explain: PPPs are price relatives for the same good.
For every rupee spent in India, 10 yen buys the same egg in Japan.

steps.prompt: Find the market exchange rate implied.

steps.answer: At market rates Japan's high prices inflate its GDP compared with India's low-price GDP
steps.explain: PPP removes price-level differences, so GDP reflects real volume.

front: A 60 W incandescent lamp (800 lm, 1,200 h life, 48.4 g CO₂/h) is replaced with an 8 W LED (800 lm, 25,000 h life, 6.4 g CO₂/h). For 4,000 operating hours a year, find the energy and CO₂ saved per year.
back: Energy saved = 208 kWh/yr; CO₂ saved = 168 kg/yr.
explain: The LED gives the same 800 lumens for about 1/8 of the power (8 W vs 60 W), which is the book's example of energy efficiency as a resource. Emissions scale with energy, so CO₂ falls by the same proportion. The LED also lasts about 20 times longer.

steps.explain: Same light output (800 lm), so the comparison is fair.

steps.prompt: Compute the CO₂ saved per hour.

front: A country produces 400 Mtoe of energy, imports 200 Mtoe, exports 50 Mtoe and withdraws a net 10 Mtoe from stocks. Its GDP at constant prices is US$ 1.4 trillion. Find gross inland consumption and energy intensity in toe per million US$.
back: Gross inland consumption = 560 Mtoe; energy intensity = 400 toe per million US$.
explain: Gross inland consumption = production + imports − exports + net stock withdrawals. Energy intensity = consumption ÷ GDP, expressed in toe per million US$, with GDP at constant prices so inflation does not distort the comparison.

steps.prompt: Write the gross inland consumption formula.
steps.answer: Production + imports − exports + net stock withdrawals

steps.explain: Exports leave the economy, so they are subtracted.
Match the units of the intensity ratio.

front: When was the Energy Conservation Act enacted, and when did BEE come into existence?
back: The EC Act was enacted in 2001 (in force from 1 March 2002). The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) was set up under it on 1 March 2002, under the Ministry of Power.
explain: BEE is the statutory body responsible for implementing the EC Act. Its mission is to develop policies and strategies, with emphasis on self-regulation and market principles, to reduce the energy intensity of the Indian economy. It does not set tariffs or give renewable capital subsidies.
source: BEE 2024 P1 Q40; BEE 2025 P1 Q40

front: Who are 'Designated Consumers' (DCs) under the EC Act, and what must they do?
back: Large energy users in energy-intensive industries and establishments notified in the Act's Schedule. They must appoint or designate a certified energy manager, get mandatory energy audits done by an accredited energy auditor, report energy consumption, and meet the specified energy consumption norms.
explain: Scheduled sectors include thermal power, cement, iron & steel, aluminium, fertilizer, pulp & paper, textile, chlor-alkali, petroleum refineries, railways and DISCOMs, among others. The threshold for each sector is notified in tonnes of oil equivalent per year. Non-compliance attracts penalties.
source: BEE 2025 P1 Q37; BEE 2024 P1 L4

front: What data do you need to check whether a plant qualifies as a Designated Consumer?
back: Annual consumption of every energy source (grid electricity in kWh, coal in t, furnace oil and HSD in litres or kL, LPG or natural gas in kg or m³) together with each fuel's calorific value (and density for liquids). Convert everything to toe and compare with the notified threshold for that sector.
explain: Total toe = Σ(quantity × GCV) ÷ 10⁷ kcal. Electricity is converted using 860 kcal/kWh. Include all purchased and self-generated energy inputs.

front: Name the main measures empowered by the Energy Conservation Act 2001.
back: Standards & Labelling of appliances, mandatory energy audits and energy managers for Designated Consumers, energy consumption norms, the Energy Conservation Building Code, and creation of BEE, State Designated Agencies and Energy Conservation Funds.
explain: The Central Government acts through BEE, and State Governments act through State Designated Agencies (SDAs), which enforce the Act at state level. Energy Saving Certificates were added by the 2010 amendment and form the basis of PAT.

front: What were the key changes made by the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022?
back: Power to set up a Carbon Credit Trading Scheme; mandatory minimum share of non-fossil (green hydrogen, biomass, renewable) energy for designated consumers; extension of the building code to large residential buildings as the Energy Conservation and Sustainable Building Code; Standards & Labelling extended to vehicles and vessels; enlarged BEE Governing Council; SERCs to adjudicate penalties.
explain: The amendment moved the Act from energy efficiency alone towards decarbonisation and India's climate commitments. It gives the legal basis for the Indian Carbon Market, which issues carbon credit certificates.

front: What penalty applies for non-compliance with EC Act provisions, as amended?
back: Up to ₹10 lakh, plus up to ₹10,000 for each day the failure continues. A Designated Consumer that fails its energy consumption norms is also liable to an additional penalty linked to the price of each excess metric toe consumed.
explain: These penalties are meant to make compliance cheaper than violation. Under the 2022 amendment, penalties are adjudicated by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission.

front: What is the objective of BEE's Standards & Labelling (S&L) programme?
back: To give consumers an informed choice about the energy and cost-saving potential of appliances, through star labels (1 to 5 stars; more stars means more efficient).
explain: Launched in 2006, S&L covers appliances such as ACs, refrigerators, motors, distribution transformers and LED lamps, some under mandatory labelling. It pushes the market towards efficient products, and thresholds are tightened over time.

front: What is the purpose of the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC)?
back: To set minimum energy-performance standards for new commercial buildings (connected load ≥ 100 kW or contract demand ≥ 120 kVA), covering envelope, HVAC, lighting, hot water and electrical systems.
explain: ECBC was first launched in 2007 and revised in 2017. A residential code (Eco-Niwas Samhita) followed, and the 2022 amendment renamed it the Energy Conservation and Sustainable Building Code. Daylight harvesting means automatically dimming artificial lighting according to available daylight, and is a typical ECBC measure.

front: What is the PAT scheme, and under which mission was it launched?
back: Perform, Achieve and Trade: a market-based mechanism under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE), one of the 8 missions of the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008). It sets mandatory SEC-reduction targets for Designated Consumers.
explain: Plants that beat their target are issued Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts). Plants that fall short must buy ESCerts or pay a penalty. ESCerts are traded on the power exchanges (IEX and PXIL).

front: What is one ESCert worth?
back: 1 Energy Saving Certificate (ESCert) = 1 tonne of oil equivalent (toe) of energy saved beyond the PAT target.
explain: Number of ESCerts = (target SEC − achieved SEC) × production in the baseline year, expressed in toe. PAT Cycle I (2012–15) covered 478 DCs in 8 sectors with a target of about 6.686 Mtoe, and achieved about 8.67 Mtoe.

front: Name the four initiatives under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE).
back: 1. PAT (Perform, Achieve and Trade). 2. MTEE (Market Transformation for Energy Efficiency). 3. EEFP (Energy Efficiency Financing Platform). 4. FEEED (Framework for Energy Efficient Economic Development).
explain: PAT sets and trades efficiency targets. MTEE speeds up the shift to efficient appliances. EEFP helps finance institutions fund EE projects. FEEED provides fiscal instruments such as risk guarantee and venture funds.

front: What is the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) 2023 for the Indian Carbon Market?
back: Notified in 2023 under the EC (Amendment) Act 2022. It has a compliance mechanism, where obligated entities get GHG-emission-intensity targets, and an offset mechanism for voluntary projects. 1 carbon credit certificate = 1 tCO₂e reduced or removed.
explain: BEE is the administrator. Grid Controller of India acts as the registry, CERC regulates trading on power exchanges, and a National Steering Committee for the Indian Carbon Market (NSC-ICM) oversees it. Obligated sectors largely carry over from PAT, moving from energy (toe) targets to emission-intensity (tCO₂e per unit of product) targets.

front: What are the Act number and date of the Energy Conservation Act, and of its 2010 amendment?
back: Act 52 of 2001, dated 29-9-2001; amended by Act No. 28 of 2010, dated 4-8-2010.
explain: The EC Act gives the legal framework and institutional arrangements for energy efficiency in India. Its first amendment came in 2010 (a frequent MCQ: options like 1948, 2003 and 2007 are distractors). The guide book (2015) reproduces the Act as amended in 2010.

front: What changes did the 2010 amendment make to the Energy Conservation Act?
back: It expanded energy conservation norms for buildings, tightened efficiency norms for appliances and equipment, and created a framework for trading energy savings between efficient and inefficient industries (energy savings certificates). It also raised penalties and provided for an Appellate Tribunal for Energy Conservation.
explain: The trading framework (Section 14A) is the legal basis of the PAT scheme. The Appellate Tribunal hears appeals against orders of the adjudicating officer, the Central or State Government, or any other authority under the Act.

front: Under the amended EC Act, what connected load or contract demand makes a commercial building a 'building' for ECBC purposes?
back: A connected load of 100 kW or a contract demand of 120 kVA and above, used or intended for commercial purposes.
explain: The definition covers structures after ECBC rules are notified under Sections 14(p) and 15(a), and includes existing structures. A common MCQ asks for the minimum connected load: 100 kW (not 100 kVA or 500 kW).

front: True or false: the EC Act's definition of 'energy audit' includes the duration of the audit.
back: False. It covers verification, monitoring and analysis of energy use, and a technical report with recommendations, cost-benefit analysis and an action plan to reduce energy consumption. Duration is not part of it.
explain: The definition sets out what an audit must contain, not how long it takes. The manner and intervals of audits are specified separately by BEE regulations under Section 13(2)(q).

front: Name five powers or functions of BEE under Section 13 of the EC Act.
back: Any five of: recommend energy consumption norms and standards; recommend issue of energy savings certificates; recommend labelling particulars; recommend notifying designated consumers; prescribe ECBC guidelines; create awareness; arrange training; strengthen consultancy; promote R&D; develop testing and certification procedures; run pilot/demonstration projects; promote innovative financing; maintain the list of accredited energy auditors; conduct the certification exam for energy managers and auditors.
explain: Note BEE mostly recommends while the Central Government notifies. BEE also specifies by regulation the qualifications for accreditation, the manner and intervals of energy audits, and the certification procedures for energy managers and auditors.

front: Under Section 14(c), how soon after a notification can the Central Government prohibit the sale of non-conforming appliances, and can this period be extended?
back: Not within six months of the notification. The Central Government may extend this by up to a further six months, for reasons recorded in writing.
explain: The grace period lets manufacturers adapt. Grounds for extension include market share and technological developments affecting the equipment.

front: Under Section 14(e), what factors does the Central Government consider when notifying a user as a designated consumer?
back: The intensity or quantity of energy consumed, the investment needed to switch to energy-efficient equipment, the industry's capacity to invest, and the availability of energy-efficient machinery and equipment.
explain: Section 14(f) also lets the Central Government alter the Schedule list of energy-intensive industries, and 14(g) lets it prescribe different norms for different DCs.

front: What does Section 14A of the EC Act provide?
back: The Central Government may issue energy savings certificates to designated consumers whose consumption is below the prescribed norms. Designated consumers above the norms may buy these certificates to comply.
explain: This is the trading mechanism added in 2010 that underpins the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme. Section 14B lets the Central Government, with BEE, prescribe the value per metric tonne of oil equivalent of energy consumed, used for penalties.

front: Name four powers of State Governments under Section 15 of the EC Act.
back: Any four of: amend ECBC to suit regional and local climate and notify it; direct building owners/occupiers that are DCs to comply with ECBC; direct DCs to get energy audits by accredited auditors; designate an agency to coordinate, regulate and enforce the Act in the State; create awareness; arrange training; encourage preferential treatment for efficient equipment; direct DCs to furnish energy consumption information; specify matters for inspection.
explain: State powers mirror many Central powers but are exercised locally through the State Designated Agency, in consultation with BEE.

front: What is the maximum penalty under Section 26(1) of the EC Act (as amended in 2010) for failing to comply with specified provisions, and for continuing failure?
back: Up to ₹10 lakh for each failure, plus up to ₹10,000 for every day the failure continues.
explain: It applies to failures under Section 14 clauses (c), (d), (h), (i), (k), (l), (r), (s) and Section 15 clauses (b), (c), (h). Figures are as in the 2010 text reproduced in the 2015 guide book; check later amendments separately.

front: What penalty does Section 26(1A) impose for not meeting the energy consumption norms under Section 14(n)?
back: Up to ₹10 lakh, plus, for continuing failure, an additional penalty of not less than the price of every metric tonne of oil equivalent of energy consumed in excess of the norms.
explain: This is the penalty that applies to PAT designated consumers who miss their SEC targets. The 'price per mtoe' is the value prescribed under Section 14B.

front: If a penalty under the EC Act is not paid, how can it be recovered?
back: As if it were an arrear of land revenue (Section 26(2)).
explain: Treating it as land revenue lets the State use its revenue-recovery powers, such as attachment of property, without separate civil proceedings.

front: Distinguish a 'designated agency' from a 'designated consumer' under the EC Act.
back: A designated agency is the body a State Government designates, in consultation with BEE, to coordinate, regulate and enforce the Act within the State. A designated consumer is an energy-intensive user notified by the Central Government that must follow norms, appoint an energy manager, get audits done and report energy use.
explain: One is a regulator and the other is regulated. DCs submit their annual energy returns and audit action reports to the designated agency, which compiles state and sectoral energy databases and gives feedback.

front: List four duties of a State Designated Agency.
back: Any four of: prepare a list of designated consumers; compile DCs' annual energy returns, audit reports and action taken; prepare state and sectoral energy databases and give feedback to DCs; create awareness; arrange training; encourage preferential treatment for efficient equipment; appoint inspecting officers; help the State Government frame rules under Section 57; establish the Energy Conservation Fund.
explain: Responsibilities (voluntary side) include spreading awareness of the Act, liaising with BEE and state departments, building staff capacity, maintaining a state website, and organising meets between energy managers, auditors and DCs.

front: What does ECBC take into account when setting norms, and who can prescribe and modify the code?
back: It sets energy requirement norms per square metre and considers the climatic region where the building is located. The Central Government prescribes the code; State Governments can modify it to suit regional and local climatic conditions.
explain: ECBC sets minimum efficiency standards for the design and construction of commercial buildings. It aims to minimise life-cycle (construction plus energy) costs while keeping function, comfort, health and productivity.

front: The term 'standards' in an energy-efficiency programme has two meanings. What are they?
back: a) Well-defined test protocols that give an accurate estimate, or relative ranking, of a product's energy performance. b) Target limits on energy performance (maximum use or minimum efficiency) based on a specified test protocol.
explain: Standards can also prohibit the sale of products below a minimum efficiency level. Labels, by contrast, are information affixed to products so consumers can make informed choices.

front: Distinguish comparative labels from endorsement labels.
back: Comparative labels let consumers compare the efficiency of all models of a product (relative energy use, e.g. star ratings). Endorsement labels mark a group of products as efficient when they meet the minimum criteria in the product schedule.
explain: The BEE star label is a comparative label. An endorsement label is a 'seal of approval' type that does not rank models against each other.

front: What do Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS) specify, and what do they not specify?
back: They specify minimum efficiency (or maximum energy consumption) that every product must achieve, that is, energy performance or output. They do not specify the technology or design details.
explain: Keeping MEPS technology-neutral lets manufacturers innovate in how they meet the level. MEPS are reviewed and raised periodically so that more efficient products become available.

front: In BEE's star rating, which star level is the most energy efficient?
back: 5 stars is the most efficient; 1 star is the least efficient.
explain: The number of stars depends on the highest pre-set energy performance threshold the appliance meets. More stars means more savings. Star rating is part of BEE's S&L programme.

front: Which four appliances came under mandatory labelling from 7 January 2010?
back: Frost-free (household) refrigerators, room air conditioners, tubular fluorescent lamps, and distribution transformers (up to 200 kVA).
explain: In the 11th Plan the S&L programme covered 18 equipment types. Others such as direct-cool refrigerators, induction motors, ceiling fans, agricultural pump sets, colour TVs, geysers, LPG stoves, DG sets and washing machines were voluntary at the time of the 2015 book.

front: A 5-star 220 L refrigerator costs Rs 17,000 and uses 204 kWh/yr. A non-star model costs Rs 10,000 and uses 520 kWh/yr. With electricity at Rs 5/kWh, find the annual energy and money savings and the simple payback on the extra cost.
back: Saves 316 kWh/yr and Rs 1,580/yr; simple payback on the Rs 7,000 extra cost ≈ 4.4 years.
explain: This is the guide book's star-rating example. Its table prints a payback of 1–1.5 years, but the book's own figures (Rs 7,000 extra ÷ Rs 1,580/yr) give about 4.4 years. The book notes the prices and consumption are assumed values for illustration.

steps.prompt: Find the annual cost of each model.

steps.explain: Payback = extra investment ÷ annual saving. The book's table shows 1–1.5 years, which does not follow from these figures.

front: What saving did BEE's pilot study show for replacing inefficient agricultural pumps with star-rated pump sets, and how is Ag-DSM implemented?
back: About 40% energy saving. Pump-set replacement is carried out by an ESCO or the distribution company on rural feeders where supply-quality improvements (feeder segregation, HVDS) have already been done.
explain: DSM means utilities managing customer demand, for example shifting load from peak to off-peak, to cut expensive peak purchases and capital needs. BEE's municipal DSM programme covers 175 municipalities with investment-grade audits and DPRs, with ESCOs encouraged to implement.

front: Explain the Bachat Lamp Yojana (BLY): what it replaced, at what price, and how the price gap was funded.
back: It replaced household incandescent bulbs with CFLs sold at about Rs 15 each (similar to a bulb's price), using the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) to recover the gap between the CFL's market price and Rs 15.
explain: 60 W and 100 W bulbs were replaced by 11–15 W and 20–25 W CFLs, giving about 80% energy saving with no loss of light. The major part of the subsidy comes from CDM revenue (carbon credits), not from DISCOMs or the central budget.

front: What is the objective of BEE's SME programme, and name example clusters.
back: To speed up adoption of energy-efficient technologies and practices in selected SME clusters through knowledge sharing, capacity building and innovative financing. It is market driven. Examples: Ahmedabad (chemicals), Surat (textiles), Warangal (rice milling).
explain: It funds need-based diagnostic studies and pilot projects at cluster level, builds the capacity of local service and technology providers, and facilitates implementation through collateral funding by lead banks.

front: State the annual energy consumption thresholds for designated consumers in these sectors: thermal power, fertilizer, cement, iron & steel, pulp & paper, chlor-alkali, aluminium, textile.
back: 30,000 toe/yr for thermal power, fertilizer, cement, iron & steel, and pulp & paper; 12,000 toe for chlor-alkali; 7,500 toe for aluminium; 3,000 toe for textile.
explain: Nine energy-intensive sectors were notified, the ninth being Railways (traction sub-stations, loco sheds, production units and workshops). DCs must appoint a certified energy manager, get mandatory audits, comply with norms and report energy use every financial year.

front: For working out a designated consumer's energy use in MTOE, what calorific basis is used, and what if the supplier gives no GCV certificate?
back: 1 kg oil equivalent = 10,000 kcal and 1 MTOE = 1 × 10⁷ kcal. Without a supplier certificate, the GCV is taken from a test certificate of a NABL-accredited, State Government or Government-recognised laboratory.
explain: Using 10,000 kcal/kg as the oil-equivalent basis is a common MCQ (not 10,500 or 9,800). Actual fuel GCVs are multiplied by quantities and divided by 10⁷ to get MTOE.

front: What is the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme, and how many DCs did its first cycle cover?
back: A market-based mechanism that sets mandatory specific energy consumption (SEC) reduction targets for energy-intensive DCs and lets units that beat their targets earn tradable energy savings certificates (ESCerts). The first cycle covered 478 DCs in 8 sectors.
explain: Sector counts: thermal power 144, textile 90, cement 85, iron & steel 67, pulp & paper 31, fertilizer 29, chlor-alkali 22, aluminium 10. The legal basis is the 2010 amendment (Section 14A).

front: How were PAT cycle-1 targets set, when was the assessment year, and how are ESCerts traded?
back: Targets were unit-specific, about 3–7% SEC reduction: smaller for already-efficient units and larger for less-efficient ones. The assessment year was 2014-15. ESCerts trade on power exchanges and can be banked for the next cycle.
explain: PAT cycle 1 started in 2012-13 and lasted three years. ESCerts issued depend on savings beyond the target in the assessment year. Units missing targets face penalty under Section 26(1A), and compliance is checked by verification and check-verification through empanelled accredited energy auditor firms.

front: What qualifications does a person need to become an Accredited Energy Auditor?
back: Be a certified energy manager who has also passed BEE's 'Energy Performance for Equipment and Utility Systems' exam; have five years of energy audit experience, at least three in energy-intensive industries; and receive a certificate of accreditation from BEE.
explain: BEE's Accreditation Advisory Committee assesses the applicant's audit experience and competence through an oral interview before granting accreditation.

front: Which earlier laws did the Electricity Act 2003 consolidate?
back: The Indian Electricity Act 1910, the Electricity (Supply) Act 1948 and the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act 1998.
explain: The Act aims to develop the electricity sector by distancing government from regulation. It consolidates the laws on generation, transmission, distribution, trading and use of electricity. The EC Act 2001, not the Electricity Act, gives the legal framework for energy efficiency.

front: List five main features of the Electricity Act 2003.
back: Any five of: generation free from licensing; captive generation free from control; restructuring of SEBs; mandatory regulatory commissions; open access in transmission; phased open access in distribution; trading recognised as a distinct activity; strict provisions on grid discipline and power theft; supply to all areas with rural provisions; rationalised tariffs.
explain: Exceptions and controls remain. CEA clearance is still needed for hydro projects (dam safety, inter-state issues), load dispatch stays with government for grid stability, and metering of all supply is mandatory.

front: What is the Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO), who sets it, and how can it be met?
back: A quota set by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions under the Electricity Act 2003. Each retail seller must buy a minimum share of power from renewable sources such as wind, solar, small hydro and biomass. It can be met by owning a renewable facility or by purchasing renewable power.
explain: Internationally it is called a Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS): a policy that guarantees a minimum amount of renewable energy in the resource portfolio.

front: According to the Integrated Energy Policy (Expert Committee, August 2006), what power capacity would India need by 2031-32?
back: Nearly 8,00,000 MW, up from about 1,60,000 MW at the time, with coal demand over 2 billion t/yr.
explain: To sustain 8% growth to 2031-32 and meet lifeline needs, primary energy supply must grow 3–4 times and electricity capacity or supply 6–7 times over 2003-04 levels. Coal remains the most important source through 2031-32, so clean-coal and in-situ gasification technologies are stressed.

front: What energy intensities does the Integrated Energy Policy quote for India and other economies, and by how much could India cut its intensity?
back: India 0.16 kgoe per dollar of GDP, against China 0.23, the US 0.22, the world 0.21, and Germany/OECD 0.17. Denmark (0.13), the UK (0.14), and Brazil and Japan (0.15) do better. Efficiency could cut India's energy intensity by up to 25%.
explain: The policy treats lower energy intensity through efficiency as an untapped domestic energy source. Key areas include mining, generation, T&D, water pumping, industrial processes, haulage, mass transport and building design.

front: What power-plant efficiency targets and procurement principle does the Integrated Energy Policy set?
back: Raise average gross generation efficiency from 30.5% to 34%. New plants should move from 36% to at least 38–40%. Government and PSUs should buy on minimum life-cycle cost rather than minimum initial cost.
explain: Other measures: benchmarks for all energy-intensive sectors, minimum fuel-efficiency standards for vehicles, urban mass transport and rail freight, and energy-efficiency specialisations and certification in technical colleges.

front: Under the Integrated Energy Policy, what should renewable-energy incentives be linked to, and what instrument was proposed?
back: Actual energy generated, not capacity installed. The proposed instrument was a Tradable Tax Rebate Certificate (TTRC), payable according to certified energy actually supplied.
explain: Other measures include feed-in laws or differential tariffs for wind, small hydro and cogeneration; RPS; and promoting fuel-wood plantations, biogas, wood gasifiers, solar thermal and PV, biodiesel and ethanol. The main long-term focus is solar.

front: How many days of oil imports does the Integrated Energy Policy recommend holding as a strategic reserve?
back: A reserve equal to 90 days of oil imports (and/or buy options on emergency supplies from large storages such as Singapore).
explain: Other energy-security recommendations: more exploration for coal, oil and gas; buffer stocks for short-term price volatility; in-situ coal gasification; coal-bed methane; enhanced oil recovery; the thorium cycle; and solar power. Redundancy guards against technical risks such as generator failure or pipeline leaks.

front: What are the three stages of India's planned nuclear power development?
back: Pressurised heavy water reactors → fast breeder reactors → thorium-based reactors.
explain: India has poor uranium resources (ore up to 0.1% U against 12–14% abroad), enough for only about 10,000 MW, which makes nuclear power 2–3 times costlier than with imported supplies. Thorium is the long-term route.

front: Name the eight National Missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008).
back: National Solar Mission; Enhanced Energy Efficiency; Sustainable Habitat; Water; Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem; Green India; Sustainable Agriculture; Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.
explain: A favourite MCQ trap: there is no 'National Mission on CFC alternatives'. NAPCC was released in 2008 to advance development while addressing adaptation and mitigation.

front: What are the four initiatives of the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE)?
back: PAT (Perform, Achieve and Trade); MTEE (Market Transformation for Energy Efficiency); EEFP (Energy Efficiency Financing Platform); FEEED (Framework for Energy Efficient Economic Development).
explain: PAT certifies and trades industrial savings. MTEE makes efficient appliances affordable (BLY, SEEP). EEFP links financial institutions, ESCOs and government to finance DSM. FEEED offers fiscal instruments: the Partial Risk Guarantee Fund (PRGFEE) and the Venture Capital Fund (VCFEE) for energy efficiency.

front: What were NMEEE's expected outcomes at full implementation?
back: Avoided capacity of 19,598 MW, fuel savings of about 23 million t/yr, and GHG reductions of 98.55 million t/yr, unlocking an energy-efficiency market of about Rs 74,000 crore.
explain: NMEEE was approved for 2010-11 and 2011-12 with an outlay of Rs 235.50 crore and continued in the XII Plan with Rs 775 crore. Earlier EC Act schemes had already avoided 10,836 MW of capacity in the XI Plan.

front: What targets do the Green India Mission and the National Water Mission set?
back: Green India: afforest 6 million hectares and raise forest and tree cover from 23% to 33% of land area. Water Mission: improve water-use efficiency by 20%.
explain: Other NAPCC facts: the Solar Mission notes 1% of India's land could meet its electricity needs till 2031. The Sustainable Habitat Mission covers building efficiency (extending ECBC), urban waste management and a shift to public transport.

front: A textile plant uses per month 7,00,000 kWh of grid electricity, 40 kL of furnace oil (SG 0.92, GCV 10,000 kcal/kg), 60 t of coal (GCV 3,450 kcal/kg) and 10 kL of HSD (SG 0.885, GCV 10,500 kcal/kg). Take 1 kWh = 860 kcal and 1 kgoe = 10,000 kcal. Find (a) monthly MTOE, (b) % share of each source, (c) whether the plant is a designated consumer.
back: (a) ≈127 MTOE/month; (b) electricity 47.4%, furnace oil 29.0%, coal 16.3%, HSD 7.3%; (c) 1,524 MTOE/yr is below the 3,000 MTOE textile threshold, so it is not a designated consumer.
explain: Convert each energy stream to kcal (volume × SG × GCV for liquids, kWh × 860 for electricity), add them and divide by 10⁷. Compare annual consumption with the notified threshold for the sector; for textiles this is 3,000 toe/yr.

steps.explain: 1 kWh = 860 kcal for the MTOE calculation.

steps.prompt: Add and convert to MTOE; find shares.

front: An aluminium unit uses 60 million kWh of grid electricity and 1,500 t of furnace oil (GCV 10,000 kcal/kg) per year. Using 1 kWh = 860 kcal and 1 MTOE = 10⁷ kcal, is it a designated consumer?
back: Total ≈ 6,660 MTOE/yr, below the 7,500 MTOE aluminium threshold, so it is not a designated consumer at this level.
explain: This uses the same MTOE method as the guide book's solved example. The answer depends on the sector: 6,660 toe would make a textile (3,000) unit a DC, but not an aluminium (7,500) or cement (30,000) unit.

steps.answer: Aluminium threshold = 7,500 MTOE/yr → 6,660 < 7,500 → not a DC

front: A designated consumer fails to comply with a direction under Section 14(h) (getting an energy audit done), and the failure continues for 20 days after it is first penalised. What is the maximum total penalty under Section 26(1) as given in the guide book?
back: ₹10 lakh + 20 × ₹10,000 = ₹12 lakh (maximum).
explain: Section 26(1) sets up to ₹10 lakh for each failure plus up to ₹10,000 per day of continuing failure. These are maximums decided by the adjudicating officer, and unpaid amounts are recovered as arrears of land revenue. Figures are from the 2010 text in the 2015 book.

steps.answer: Section 26(1): failure under Section 14(h) is listed
steps.explain: 26(1A) applies only to failure under 14(n), the energy norms.
Recoverable as arrear of land revenue if unpaid.

front: 1 tonne of oil equivalent (toe) equals how many kcal and MJ?
explain: toe is the common unit BEE uses to add up different fuels; for example Designated Consumer thresholds and PAT targets are in toe. Convert each fuel to kcal (quantity × GCV) and divide by 10⁷. For example, 2,500 kg of coal at 4,000 kcal/kg = 10⁷ kcal = 1 toe.
source: BEE 2025 P1 Q6; BEE 2024 P1 Q33

front: What are the energy equivalents of 1 kWh and 1 kcal?
back: 1 kWh = 860 kcal = 3,600 kJ (3.6 MJ); 1 kcal = 4.187 kJ.
explain: These conversions are used in almost every Paper 1 numerical. To convert a thermal load in kcal/h to electrical kW, divide by 860. To convert electrical energy to toe, multiply kWh by 860 and divide by 10⁷.

front: Which of these is NOT equal to 1 atm: 101.3 kPa, 10,332 mmWC, 14.7 psi, 0.98 kg/cm²?
back: 0.98 kg/cm² is wrong. 1 atm ≈ 1.033 kg/cm² (101.325 kPa = 10,332 mmWC = 14.7 psi = 760 mmHg).
explain: 1 kg/cm² ≈ 0.98 bar, which is easy to confuse. Remember 1 atm = 1.01325 bar ≈ 1.033 kg/cm², slightly more than 1 kg/cm².

front: State the relation between gauge pressure, absolute (system) pressure and atmospheric pressure.
back: Gauge pressure = Absolute (system) pressure − Atmospheric pressure, i.e. pg = ps − pa.
explain: Pressure gauges read relative to the surrounding atmosphere, so a gauge open to air reads zero. Steam tables use absolute pressure, so add about 1.013 bar to a gauge reading before looking up properties.

front: What property does 'Redwood seconds' measure?
back: Viscosity. It is the time in seconds for a fixed volume of oil to flow through a standard orifice of the Redwood viscometer.
explain: Viscosity matters for fuel oils because it sets the pumping and atomisation temperature. Furnace oil is preheated to bring its viscosity down to the level the burner needs.

front: Which common substance has the highest specific heat, and what is its value?
back: Water, at about 1 kcal/kg°C (4.187 kJ/kg·K). It is far higher than metals such as iron (~0.11), mercury (~0.033) or lead (~0.03).
explain: Water's high specific heat makes it an excellent heat-transfer and storage medium, used in cooling towers, hot-water systems and chilled water. Heating 500 litres of water (500 kg) by 6°C needs 500 × 1 × 6 = 3,000 kcal, which is about 12,560 kJ.
source: BEE 2025 P1 Q7, Q10; BEE 2024 P1 Q8

front: What is the formula for sensible heat, and how does latent heat differ?
back: Sensible heat Q = m × Cp × ΔT, which changes temperature without a change of phase. Latent heat Q = m × L, which changes phase (e.g. boiling or condensing) at constant temperature.
explain: Example: cooling 2,000 kg of water by 10°C removes 2,000 × 1 × 10 = 20,000 kcal of sensible heat. Condensing steam releases its latent heat (about 540 kcal/kg at atmospheric pressure), which is why steam is such an effective heating medium.

front: What is the dryness fraction (x) of dry saturated steam, and what does x < 1 mean?
back: x = 1 for dry saturated steam (BEE also gives x = 1 for superheated steam). x < 1 means wet steam that carries water droplets: x = mass of dry steam ÷ total mass.
explain: Wet steam has less usable enthalpy per kg (hf + x·hfg). It also causes erosion and poorer heat transfer, so steam traps and separators are used to keep steam dry.

front: How do you calculate the number of moles in a given mass? (e.g. 72 g or 54 g of water)
back: Moles = mass ÷ molecular weight. Water (H₂O) has a molecular weight of 18, so 72 g = 4 mol and 54 g = 3 mol.
explain: Mole calculations underpin combustion stoichiometry. For example, C + O₂ → CO₂ means 12 kg of carbon gives 44 kg of CO₂, so emissions = carbon × 44/12.
source: BEE 2024 P1 Q9; BEE 2025 P1 Q46

front: What is the mean molecular weight of air (77% N₂, 23% O₂ by weight)?
explain: When composition is given by weight, use the harmonic mean: M = 1 ÷ Σ(wᵢ/Mᵢ). By volume, air is about 79% N₂ and 21% O₂, and the mole-weighted average gives the same ≈ 28.8–29.

front: Which fuel has the largest difference between GCV and NCV, and why?
back: Natural gas. Its high hydrogen content forms a lot of water vapour on combustion, and the latent heat of that vapour is counted in GCV but not in NCV.
explain: GCV (HHV) assumes the water vapour in flue gas is condensed and its latent heat recovered. NCV (LHV) assumes it leaves as vapour. Fuels rich in hydrogen (natural gas, LPG) or moisture show the biggest gap. BEE efficiency calculations conventionally use GCV.

front: Rank LPG, diesel, furnace oil and bagasse by calorific value. Which is lowest?
back: Bagasse is lowest (roughly 2,200–2,300 kcal/kg as fired, because of about 50% moisture). LPG is highest (~11,000+ kcal/kg). Diesel and furnace oil are about 10,000–10,800 kcal/kg.
explain: Biomass fuels such as bagasse and rice husk have low calorific value because of moisture and ash. They still matter as low-cost renewable fuels for sugar mills and cogeneration.

front: What two measurements are needed to find the relative humidity of air with a psychrometer?
back: Dry Bulb Temperature (DBT) and Wet Bulb Temperature (WBT). RH is then read from a psychrometric chart. A sling psychrometer measures both.
explain: DBT indicates the sensible heat content of the air-water vapour mixture. The wet-bulb depression (DBT − WBT) shows how dry the air is. When the depression is zero, no evaporation is possible and RH = 100%.

front: What happens to the relative humidity when air is heated without changing its moisture content (absolute humidity)?
back: RH decreases, because warmer air can hold more moisture at saturation while the actual moisture stays the same.
explain: This is the principle of pre-heating air before a dryer: it lowers RH and increases the air's capacity to pick up moisture. Cooling air at constant moisture raises RH until it reaches 100% at the dew point.

front: Define power factor. What is the PF of a circuit with resistive and inductive load?
back: PF = kW ÷ kVA = cos φ. A resistive + inductive (R-L) circuit has a lagging PF of less than 1. Also, kVA² = kW² + kVAr².
explain: Inductive loads such as motors and transformers draw reactive power (kVAr) for their magnetic fields. That raises kVA and current for the same kW, which increases I²R losses and kVA-based demand charges. Capacitors supply kVAr locally to improve PF. Only a pure resistance gives unity PF.

front: An induction motor nameplate says 30 kW, 85% efficiency. How much power does it draw at full load?
back: 35.29 kW. The nameplate kW is shaft output, so input = 30 ÷ 0.85 = 35.29 kW.
explain: Motor ratings always state mechanical output. Electrical input = output ÷ efficiency. Audits compare measured input kW with rated input to estimate percentage loading.

front: How does wind turbine power vary with wind speed, and what is the formula?
back: P = ½ ρ A V³, so power varies with the cube of wind speed: tripling the speed gives 27× the power.
explain: For example, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, A = 200 m² and V = 8 m/s gives 0.5 × 1.2 × 200 × 512 ≈ 61.4 kW available in the wind. A turbine captures only part of this, with the Betz limit at 59.3%. Yaw control turns the rotor to face the wind, and pitch control adjusts the blade angle.

front: Roughly what voltage does a single silicon PV cell produce, and what is its working principle?
back: About 0.5 V. It works by the photovoltaic effect: photons create electron-hole pairs at a p-n junction, which produces DC current.
explain: Cells are connected in series and parallel in modules to reach usable voltage and power. Cell efficiency = maximum power output ÷ (insolation × cell area), so it does not depend on the inverter. An inverter converts DC to AC.

front: What are the reactants and by-product in a hydrogen fuel cell?
back: Hydrogen combines electrochemically with oxygen to generate electricity, and water is the by-product (plus heat).
explain: A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electricity without combustion, so it is not limited by Carnot efficiency. Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode, and oxygen is reduced at the cathode.

front: What is the composition of producer gas, and how is gasifier efficiency calculated?
back: Producer gas is mainly CO, H₂ and CH₄ (combustible), diluted with N₂ and CO₂. Gasifier efficiency = (gas volume × gas CV) ÷ (biomass mass × biomass CV).
explain: Example: 1 kg of wood at 4,000 kcal/kg giving 2 m³ of gas at 1,000 kcal/m³ → 2,000/4,000 = 50% efficiency. Producer gas has a low CV (about 1,000–1,200 kcal/Nm³) because it contains a lot of nitrogen from the air.

front: Solar radiation reaching the earth consists of which bands?
back: Ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation.
explain: Roughly half of solar energy is in the infrared and most of the rest is visible light. A small part is ultraviolet, most of which is absorbed by stratospheric ozone.

front: A plant uses in one year: 12 million kWh of grid electricity; 1,500 kL of furnace oil (density 0.93 kg/L, GCV 10,200 kcal/kg); and 8,000 t of coal (GCV 4,000 kcal/kg). It produces 20,000 t of product. Find the total annual energy use in toe and the specific energy consumption in toe/t. Take 1 kWh = 860 kcal.
back: Total ≈ 5,655 toe per year; SEC ≈ 0.283 toe/t of product.
explain: Converting every energy source to toe through kcal is exactly how a plant checks whether it qualifies as a Designated Consumer, and how SEC is reported under PAT. Coal is the biggest share here, about 57% of the total.

steps.explain: Mass = volume × density; energy = mass × GCV.

front: Distinguish potential energy and kinetic energy, and give two forms of each.
back: Potential energy is stored energy due to position or configuration (forms: chemical, nuclear, stored mechanical, gravitational). Kinetic energy is energy of motion (forms: radiant, thermal, motion, sound, electrical).
explain: Examples: a raised pile-driver head has potential energy of position; a compressed spring has potential energy of configuration. A moving vehicle, flowing fluid or moving machine parts have kinetic energy.

front: Give the formulas for gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy and nuclear (mass-energy) energy.
back: PE = m g h; KE = ½ m v²; E = m c² (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s).
explain: In fission, a uranium nucleus splits and loses a little mass, which is released as energy according to Einstein's equation. Because c² is so large, a tiny mass loss gives an enormous amount of energy.

front: Which is an example of stored mechanical energy: water in a reservoir, an arrow in a stretched bow, an airborne aeroplane, or you on a mountain top?
back: An arrow in a stretched bow. Stored mechanical energy is energy stored in objects by applying a force, like compressed springs or stretched rubber bands.
explain: Water in a reservoir and a person on a mountain are examples of gravitational (position) energy. An airborne aeroplane has both kinetic and gravitational energy. This is a frequent MCQ.

front: How do radiant energy and sound energy differ in the way they travel?
back: Radiant energy is electromagnetic energy travelling in transverse waves (light, X-rays, gamma rays, radio waves; solar energy is an example). Sound travels through substances as longitudinal (compression/rarefaction) waves.
explain: Radiant energy needs no medium, so it crosses the vacuum of space from the sun. Sound needs a material medium. Thermal energy is the vibration and movement of atoms and molecules, for example geothermal energy.

front: Define the joule and the watt, and give the formula for the power of a rotating shaft.
back: 1 J = work done when a 1 N force moves through 1 m in its direction (1 N·m). 1 W = 1 J/s. For a rotating shaft, P = T ω = 2πTN/60 (T in N·m, N in rpm).
explain: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t, so energy W = P t. For large quantities the units are MJ (10⁶ J), GJ (10⁹ J), TJ (10¹² J) and PJ (10¹⁵ J). Work done by a rotating body is W = T·θ, with θ in radians.

front: A portable machine needs a force of 200 N to move it. How much work is done moving it 20 m, and what average power is used if this takes 25 s? (Example 3.1)
back: Work = 4,000 J (4 kJ); power = 160 W.
explain: Work = force × distance in the direction of the force; power = work ÷ time. 1 J/s = 1 W.

steps.explain: Work done by a constant force along its line of action.

front: How many times per second does the current reverse direction in a 50 Hz AC supply?
back: 100 times per second (twice every cycle).
explain: DC is unidirectional and non-varying, like a battery's output. AC reverses at regular intervals. The normal utility supply frequency in India is 50 Hz.

front: An electric heater consumes 1.8 MJ when connected to a 250 V supply for 30 minutes. Find its power rating and the current it draws. (Example 3.2)
back: Power = 1,000 W (1 kW); current = 4 A.
explain: Power = energy ÷ time (time in seconds). Then use P = V I for the current.

steps.explain: SI units: J and s give W.

front: A 100 W bulb is connected to a 250 V supply. Find (a) the current and (b) the resistance of the bulb. (Example 3.3)
explain: Use P = V I for current, then Ohm's law R = V/I. The book repeats the same problem as Example 3.5, with the unit misprinted there as W instead of Ω.

front: An electric kettle has a resistance of 30 Ω. What current flows on a 240 V supply, and what is its power rating? (Example 3.4)
back: Current = 8 A; power = 1,920 W (1.92 kW).
explain: Ohm's law gives the current, and P = V I gives the power. You could also use P = V²/R = 240²/30 = 1,920 W.

front: A 230 V, 5 kW electric heater is used for hot water. Find the electricity consumed per hour (a) at rated voltage, (b) at 200 V. (Example 3.6)
back: (a) 5 kWh; (b) about 3.78 kWh.
explain: A resistive heater's power varies with the square of voltage (P = V²/R), so P at 200 V = 5 × (200/230)² = 3.78 kW. The book's printed working shows (200/230) × 5 without the square, but its answer of 3.78 kWh is the squared result.

steps.prompt: State how heater power varies with voltage.
steps.answer: P = V²/R, so P ∝ V² (resistance constant)
steps.explain: The heater is a fixed resistance.
Low voltage also means less heat output, so heating takes longer.

front: Write the power-triangle relationships between kW, kVA, kVAr and power factor.
back: kW = kVA cos φ; kVA = kW / cos φ; kVAr = kVA sin φ; PF = cos φ; also kW = √(kVA² − kVAr²).
explain: Active (resistive) power does useful work. Reactive power builds the magnetic flux of inductive devices but is otherwise not usable. Apparent power is the hypotenuse. Only components in the same phase can be added, kW to kW and kVAr to kVAr. In an MCQ, all three expressions for active power are correct ('all of the above').

front: What usually causes current to lag voltage in an AC system?
back: Inductive load, for example motors and transformers, which need reactive current to build their magnetic fields.
explain: A purely resistive load keeps current in phase with voltage, while a capacitive load makes current lead. Lagging reactive power (kVAr) is what lowers the power factor of typical industrial loads.

front: Give the power formulas for balanced three-phase and single-phase loads.
back: Three-phase: P = √3 × V_L × I_L × cos φ. Single-phase: P = V × I × cos φ (V_L = line voltage, I_L = line current).
explain: In industry, single-phase power is mostly used for lighting, fractional-HP motors and electric heaters. Larger motors and process loads are three-phase.

front: A 400 W mercury vapour lamp runs 10 h/day on 230 V, drawing 2 A at PF 0.8. Find the energy consumed per day. (Example 3.7)
back: About 3.7 kWh per day.
explain: For a single-phase AC load, kW = V × I × cos φ / 1,000. Multiply by hours for kWh. The measured input (0.368 kW) is a little below the nameplate 400 W.

steps.answer: kWh = V (kV) × I × cos φ × hours
steps.explain: Single-phase AC power includes power factor.

front: How do you convert a motor's horsepower rating to input kVA?
back: kVA = (HP × 0.746) / (η × PF), where η is motor efficiency and PF is motor power factor.
explain: HP × 0.746 gives output kW. Dividing by efficiency gives input kW, and dividing by PF gives kVA. Smaller motors running at part load are the least efficient and have the lowest power factor.

front: Does a motor's nameplate kW/HP rating show input or output? What about its nameplate volts, amps and PF?
back: Nameplate kW/HP is the output (shaft) power at full load. Nameplate volts, amps and PF describe input conditions at full load.
explain: This is why rated input kW is calculated as √3 × V × I × PF from nameplate values, and the rated efficiency is output kW ÷ that input. Mixing up the two is a common exam trap.
